claim: Metabolic homeostasis requires coordination between circadian clocks in different tissues.
source: Metabolic homeostasis requires coordination between circadian clocks in different tissues.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract presenting a general principle about metabolic homeostasis and circadian clocks.

claim: Systemic signals appear to be required for some transcriptional rhythms in the mammalian liver.
source: Also, systemic signals appear to be required for some transcriptional rhythms in the mammalian liver and the Drosophila fat body.
evidence: This statement references existing knowledge about transcriptional rhythms in mammalian liver requiring systemic signals.

claim: Systemic signals appear to be required for some transcriptional rhythms in the Drosophila fat body.
source: Also, systemic signals appear to be required for some transcriptional rhythms in the mammalian liver and the Drosophila fat body.
evidence: This statement references existing knowledge about transcriptional rhythms in Drosophila fat body requiring systemic signals.

claim: Free-running oscillations of the fat body clock require clock function in the PDF-positive cells of the fly brain.
source: Here we show that free-running oscillations of the fat body clock require clock function in the PDF-positive cells of the fly brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing that disrupting clocks in PDF-positive cells abolishes per rhythms in the fat body in constant darkness.

claim: Rhythmic expression of sxe1 in the fat body depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
source: Interestingly, rhythmic expression of the cytochrome P450 transcripts, sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1) and Cyp6a21, which cycle in the fat body independently of the local clock, depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing that expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 abolishes rhythmic sxe1 expression.

claim: Rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 in the fat body depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
source: Interestingly, rhythmic expression of the cytochrome P450 transcripts, sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1) and Cyp6a21, which cycle in the fat body independently of the local clock, depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing that expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 dampens rhythmic Cyp6a21 expression.

claim: sxe1 cycles in the fat body independently of the local clock.
source: Interestingly, rhythmic expression of the cytochrome P450 transcripts, sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1) and Cyp6a21, which cycle in the fat body independently of the local clock, depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Xu et al., 2011) showing that some fat body genes cycle independently of the fat body clock.

claim: Cyp6a21 cycles in the fat body independently of the local clock.
source: Interestingly, rhythmic expression of the cytochrome P450 transcripts, sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1) and Cyp6a21, which cycle in the fat body independently of the local clock, depends upon clocks in neurons expressing neuropeptide F (NPF).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work (Xu et al., 2011) showing that some fat body genes cycle independently of the fat body clock.

claim: NPF signaling is required to drive cycling of sxe1 in the fat body.
source: NPF signaling itself is required to drive cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 in the fat body, and its mammalian ortholog, Npy, functions similarly to regulate cycling of cytochrome P450 genes in the mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that npfr mutants lack rhythmic sxe1 expression.

claim: NPF signaling is required to drive cycling of Cyp6a21 in the fat body.
source: NPF signaling itself is required to drive cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 in the fat body, and its mammalian ortholog, Npy, functions similarly to regulate cycling of cytochrome P450 genes in the mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that npfr mutants lack rhythmic Cyp6a21 expression.

claim: Npy regulates cycling of cytochrome P450 genes in the mouse liver.
source: NPF signaling itself is required to drive cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 in the fat body, and its mammalian ortholog, Npy, functions similarly to regulate cycling of cytochrome P450 genes in the mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Cyp2b10 and other cytochrome P450 genes do not cycle in Npy knockout mice.

claim: Npy is the mammalian ortholog of NPF.
source: NPF signaling itself is required to drive cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 in the fat body, and its mammalian ortholog, Npy, functions similarly to regulate cycling of cytochrome P450 genes in the mouse liver.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of orthology between Drosophila NPF and mammalian Npy.

claim: NPF/Npy has a novel and conserved role in circadian rhythms.
source: These data highlight the importance of neuronal clocks for peripheral rhythms, particularly in a specific detoxification pathway, and identify a novel and conserved role for NPF/Npy in circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings in both flies and mice showing NPF/Npy regulation of peripheral gene expression.

claim: Circadian clocks constitute an endogenous timekeeping system that synchronizes behavior and physiology to changes in the physical environment.
source: Circadian clocks constitute an endogenous timekeeping system that synchronizes behavior and physiology to changes in the physical environment, such as day and night, imposed by the 24 hr rotation of the earth (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012).
evidence: This is a general statement about circadian clocks supported by citation to a review article.

claim: A coherent circadian system is composed of a cooperative network of tissue-specific circadian clocks.
source: A coherent circadian system is composed of a cooperative network of tissue-specific circadian clocks, which temporally coordinate and compartmentalize biochemical processes in the organism (Wijnen and Young, 2006).
evidence: This is a general principle about circadian systems supported by citation.

claim: Clock disruption is associated with cancer.
source: Clock disruption is associated with numerous deleterious health consequences including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders (Marcheva et al., 2010; Marcheva et al., 2013; Turek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing associations between clock disruption and health consequences.

claim: Clock disruption is associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: Clock disruption is associated with numerous deleterious health consequences including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders (Marcheva et al., 2010; Marcheva et al., 2013; Turek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing associations between clock disruption and health consequences.

claim: Clock disruption is associated with metabolic disorders.
source: Clock disruption is associated with numerous deleterious health consequences including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders (Marcheva et al., 2010; Marcheva et al., 2013; Turek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing associations between clock disruption and health consequences.

claim: The neuronal clock network in Drosophila melanogaster is comprised of roughly 150 circadian neurons.
source: In the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, the neuronal clock network is comprised of roughly 150 circadian neurons, which are grouped based on their anatomical location and function in the brain (Allada and Chung, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neuronal clock network supported by citation.

claim: The small LNvs are necessary and sufficient for rest:activity rhythms under constant conditions.
source: The small LNvs (sLNvs) have traditionally been referred to as the central clock because they are necessary and sufficient for rest:activity rhythms under constant conditions (Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004), but recent studies also indicate an important role for the LNds (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the role of sLNvs in rest:activity rhythms.

claim: The LNds have an important role in rest:activity rhythms.
source: The small LNvs (sLNvs) have traditionally been referred to as the central clock because they are necessary and sufficient for rest:activity rhythms under constant conditions (Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004), but recent studies also indicate an important role for the LNds (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study showing the role of LNds.

claim: The LNvs express the neuropeptide pigment dispersing factor (PDF).
source: The LNvs express the neuropeptide pigment dispersing factor (PDF), which is important for rest:activity rhythms (Renn et al., 1999; Stoleru et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2004; Yoshii et al., 2009) and for the function of circadian clocks in some peripheral tissues (Myers et al., 2003; Krupp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PDF is important for rest:activity rhythms.
source: The LNvs express the neuropeptide pigment dispersing factor (PDF), which is important for rest:activity rhythms (Renn et al., 1999; Stoleru et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2004; Yoshii et al., 2009) and for the function of circadian clocks in some peripheral tissues (Myers et al., 2003; Krupp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating PDF's role in rest:activity rhythms.

claim: PDF is important for the function of circadian clocks in some peripheral tissues.
source: The LNvs express the neuropeptide pigment dispersing factor (PDF), which is important for rest:activity rhythms (Renn et al., 1999; Stoleru et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2004; Yoshii et al., 2009) and for the function of circadian clocks in some peripheral tissues (Myers et al., 2003; Krupp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing PDF's role in peripheral clocks.

claim: The LNds constitute a heterogeneous group of neurons differentiated by the expression of peptides and receptors.
source: The LNds constitute a heterogeneous group of neurons differentiated by the expression of peptides and receptors (Lee et al., 2006; Johard et al., 2009; Yao and Shafer, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LNd peptides include Neuropeptide F (NPF).
source: Thus far, these peptides, which include Neuropeptide F (NPF), have only been implicated in behavioral rhythms (He et al., 2013a; Hermann et al., 2012; Hermann-Luibl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NPF has been implicated in behavioral rhythms.
source: Thus far, these peptides, which include Neuropeptide F (NPF), have only been implicated in behavioral rhythms (He et al., 2013a; Hermann et al., 2012; Hermann-Luibl et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing NPF's role in behavioral rhythms.

claim: The fat body is a tissue analogous to mammalian liver and adipose tissue.
source: For instance, a peripheral clock located in the fat body, a tissue analogous to mammalian liver and adipose tissue (Arrese and Soulages, 2010), regulates feeding behavior (Xu et al., 2008; Seay and Thummel, 2011) and nutrient storage (Xu et al., 2008) and drives the rhythmic expression of genes involved in metabolism, detoxification, innate immunity, and reproduction (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The fat body clock regulates feeding behavior.
source: For instance, a peripheral clock located in the fat body, a tissue analogous to mammalian liver and adipose tissue (Arrese and Soulages, 2010), regulates feeding behavior (Xu et al., 2008; Seay and Thummel, 2011) and nutrient storage (Xu et al., 2008) and drives the rhythmic expression of genes involved in metabolism, detoxification, innate immunity, and reproduction (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the fat body clock's role in feeding behavior.

claim: The fat body clock regulates nutrient storage.
source: For instance, a peripheral clock located in the fat body, a tissue analogous to mammalian liver and adipose tissue (Arrese and Soulages, 2010), regulates feeding behavior (Xu et al., 2008; Seay and Thummel, 2011) and nutrient storage (Xu et al., 2008) and drives the rhythmic expression of genes involved in metabolism, detoxification, innate immunity, and reproduction (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing the fat body clock's role in nutrient storage.

claim: The fat body clock drives the rhythmic expression of genes involved in metabolism, detoxification, innate immunity, and reproduction.
source: For instance, a peripheral clock located in the fat body, a tissue analogous to mammalian liver and adipose tissue (Arrese and Soulages, 2010), regulates feeding behavior (Xu et al., 2008; Seay and Thummel, 2011) and nutrient storage (Xu et al., 2008) and drives the rhythmic expression of genes involved in metabolism, detoxification, innate immunity, and reproduction (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing fat body gene expression.

claim: Molecular clocks in the brain and fat body have different effects on metabolism.
source: Molecular clocks in the brain and fat body have different effects on metabolism, suggesting that clocks in these two tissues complement each other to maintain metabolic homeostasis (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study comparing brain and fat body clock effects on metabolism.

claim: 40% of rhythmically expressed fat body transcripts are unperturbed by the absence of a functional fat body clock.
source: In addition, the fat body clock does not regulate all circadian fat body transcripts. 40% of rhythmically expressed fat body transcripts are unperturbed by the absence of a functional fat body clock (Xu et al., 2011), suggesting these genes are controlled by rhythmic external factors, which could include light, food, and/or signals from clocks in other tissues (Wijnen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing fat body gene expression in clock mutants.

claim: Fat body clock-independent genes may be controlled by rhythmic external factors such as light, food, and/or signals from clocks in other tissues.
source: In addition, the fat body clock does not regulate all circadian fat body transcripts. 40% of rhythmically expressed fat body transcripts are unperturbed by the absence of a functional fat body clock (Xu et al., 2011), suggesting these genes are controlled by rhythmic external factors, which could include light, food, and/or signals from clocks in other tissues (Wijnen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the observation that some genes cycle without the fat body clock.

claim: Cyclic expression of many liver genes persists when the liver clock is ablated.
source: Likewise in the mammalian liver, where circadian gene regulation has been well-studied, cyclic expression of many genes persists when the liver clock is ablated (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing liver gene expression in liver clock mutants.

claim: Brain specific rescue of clock function in ClockΔ19 animals partially restored liver gene expression rhythms (~40%).
source: Brain specific rescue of clock function in ClockΔ19 animals partially restored liver gene expression rhythms (~40%), albeit with compromised amplitude (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing brain clock rescue effects on liver gene expression.

claim: A majority of Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies had arrhythmic locomotor activity in constant darkness.
source: Behavioral assays of Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies showed that a majority of the flies had arrhythmic locomotor activity in constant darkness (DD) (Figure 1A and Table 1), confirming that CLKΔ expression in the LNvs disrupts circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: CLKΔ expression in the LNvs disrupts circadian rhythms.
source: Behavioral assays of Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies showed that a majority of the flies had arrhythmic locomotor activity in constant darkness (DD) (Figure 1A and Table 1), confirming that CLKΔ expression in the LNvs disrupts circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing arrhythmic behavior in Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies.

claim: Circadian expression of per in the fat body was not altered in flies with a disrupted central clock (Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ) under a 12 hr light: 12 hr dark (LD) cycle.
source: We found that circadian expression of per in the fat body was not altered in flies with a disrupted central clock (Pdf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ) under a 12 hr light: 12 hr dark (LD) cycle (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Peripheral clocks in Drosophila can detect light.
source: Unlike mammals, peripheral clocks in Drosophila can detect light, which acts as the dominant entrainment signal (Plautz et al., 1997; Oishi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Light acts as the dominant entrainment signal for peripheral clocks in Drosophila.
source: Unlike mammals, peripheral clocks in Drosophila can detect light, which acts as the dominant entrainment signal (Plautz et al., 1997; Oishi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rhythmic gene expression dampens under constant conditions and is undetectable in the fat body by the sixth day of DD.
source: Since rhythmic gene expression dampens under constant conditions and is undetectable in the fat body by the sixth day of DD (Xu et al., 2011), we tested rhythmic expression of per on the second day in DD (DD2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: per levels were rhythmic in the fat body of control flies on DD2.
source: per levels were rhythmic in the fat body of control flies on DD2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies expressing CLKΔ in the LNvs showed an apparent lack of per rhythms in the fat body on DD2.
source: In contrast, flies expressing CLKΔ in the LNvs showed an apparent lack of per rhythms in the fat body (Figure 1D; see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The clock in PDF-positive LNvs influences the peripheral fat body clock in the absence of external environmental cues.
source: This suggests that the clock in PDF-positive LNvs influences the peripheral fat body clock in the absence of external environmental cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing loss of per rhythms in DD2 when PDF-positive cells lack functional clocks.

claim: The fat body clock regulates roughly 60% of circadian genes in the fat body.
source: The fat body clock regulates roughly 60% of circadian genes in the fat body; the mechanisms that drive daily cycling of the other 40% of circadian genes in this tissue are unknown (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Many tissues in Drosophila have photoreceptors.
source: As noted above, many tissues in Drosophila have photoreceptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila tissues.

claim: LD cycles can drive rhythmic transcription via clock-independent pathways.
source: Therefore, in addition to entraining clocks to the external environment, LD cycles can drive rhythmic transcription via clock-independent pathways (Wijnen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LD cycles can drive a rhythm of feeding.
source: LD cycles can even drive a rhythm of feeding (Xu et al., 2008), which could lead to cyclic expression of metabolic genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Nutrients are known to be strong entrainment signals in peripheral tissues.
source: Nutrients are known to be strong entrainment signals in peripheral tissues; in fact, rhythmic or restricted feeding, even in the absence of a clock, can drive cyclic expression of several fat body genes (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Rhythmic or restricted feeding, even in the absence of a clock, can drive cyclic expression of several fat body genes.
source: Nutrients are known to be strong entrainment signals in peripheral tissues; in fact, rhythmic or restricted feeding, even in the absence of a clock, can drive cyclic expression of several fat body genes (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Clkjrk mutants lack functional clocks in all tissues due to a premature stop codon that eliminates the CLK activation domain.
source: To differentiate between light, nutrient, and clock control, we measured daily expression of genes that cycle independently of the fat body clock in Clkjrk mutants. Clkjrk mutants lack functional clocks in all tissues due to a premature stop codon that eliminates the CLK activation domain (Allada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Clkjrk mutation supported by citation.

claim: Clkjrk mutants cannot sustain feeding rhythms under constant conditions.
source: Although Clkjrk mutants cannot sustain feeding rhythms under constant conditions, LD cycles can drive feeding rhythms in Clkjrk flies albeit with a delayed phase relative to wild type flies (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LD cycles can drive feeding rhythms in Clkjrk flies albeit with a delayed phase relative to wild type flies.
source: Although Clkjrk mutants cannot sustain feeding rhythms under constant conditions, LD cycles can drive feeding rhythms in Clkjrk flies albeit with a delayed phase relative to wild type flies (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: None of the tested fat body clock-independent genes displayed circadian rhythms in Clkjrk mutants.
source: We found that none of these genes displayed circadian rhythms in Clkjrk mutants, suggesting that although these genes do not require an intact fat body clock, they do require an intact clock in some other tissue (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fat body clock-independent genes require an intact clock in some other tissue.
source: We found that none of these genes displayed circadian rhythms in Clkjrk mutants, suggesting that although these genes do not require an intact fat body clock, they do require an intact clock in some other tissue (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these genes cycle in fat body clock mutants but not in global clock mutants.

claim: Rhythmic gene expression of sxe2 was eliminated in Clkjrk mutants to produce an intermediate level of gene expression throughout the day.
source: Rhythmic gene expression of sex-specific enzyme 2 (sxe2), a lipase and CG17562, an oxidoreductase was eliminated in Clkjrk mutants to produce an intermediate level of gene expression throughout the day (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Rhythmic gene expression of CG17562 was eliminated in Clkjrk mutants to produce an intermediate level of gene expression throughout the day.
source: Rhythmic gene expression of sex-specific enzyme 2 (sxe2), a lipase and CG17562, an oxidoreductase was eliminated in Clkjrk mutants to produce an intermediate level of gene expression throughout the day (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Rhythmic expression as well as overall levels of sxe1 were greatly reduced in Clkjrk mutants.
source: In contrast, rhythmic expression as well as overall levels of sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1), a cytochrome P450, and CG14934, a purported glucosidase involved in glycogen breakdown, were greatly reduced in Clkjrk mutants (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Rhythmic expression as well as overall levels of CG14934 were greatly reduced in Clkjrk mutants.
source: In contrast, rhythmic expression as well as overall levels of sex-specific enzyme 1 (sxe1), a cytochrome P450, and CG14934, a purported glucosidase involved in glycogen breakdown, were greatly reduced in Clkjrk mutants (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: sxe1 was named on the basis of its regulation by the sex determination pathway in fly heads.
source: sxe1 was named on the basis of its regulation by the sex determination pathway in fly heads and is enriched in the non-neuronal fat body tissue of males (Fujii and Amrein, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: sxe1 is enriched in the non-neuronal fat body tissue of males.
source: sxe1 was named on the basis of its regulation by the sex determination pathway in fly heads and is enriched in the non-neuronal fat body tissue of males (Fujii and Amrein, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Early microarray studies indicated that sxe1 is regulated by the circadian system.
source: Early microarray studies looking for cycling transcripts in Drosophila heads also indicated that sxe1 is regulated by the circadian system (Claridge-Chang et al., 2001; McDonald and Rosbash, 2001; Ceriani et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous microarray studies.

claim: sxe1 is implicated in xenobiotic detoxification.
source: sxe1 is implicated in xenobiotic detoxification and male courtship behavior (Fujii et al., 2008) and may confer cyclic regulation to either or both of these processes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: sxe1 is implicated in male courtship behavior.
source: sxe1 is implicated in xenobiotic detoxification and male courtship behavior (Fujii et al., 2008) and may confer cyclic regulation to either or both of these processes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Abolishing the clock in PDF cells by expressing CLKΔ under Pdf-GAL4 slightly decreased sxe1 transcript levels in the abdominal fat body, but did not abolish rhythmic expression.
source: Abolishing the clock in PDF cells by expressing CLKΔ under Pdf-GAL4, slightly decreased sxe1 transcript levels in the abdominal fat body, but did not abolish rhythmic expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PDF neurons are not the primary drivers of rhythmic sxe1 expression.
source: This suggests that although the PDF neurons regulate the fat body clock, these neurons are not the primary drivers of rhythmic sxe1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting PDF neurons does not abolish sxe1 rhythms.

claim: DN1s were recently shown to be part of an output circuit regulating rest:activity rhythms.
source: In fact, DN1s were recently shown to be part of an output circuit regulating rest:activity rhythms (Cavanaugh et al., 2014), and clocks in the DN1s are known to mediate other circadian behaviors, such as aspects of the male sex drive rhythm (Fujii and Amrein 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Clocks in the DN1s are known to mediate aspects of the male sex drive rhythm.
source: In fact, DN1s were recently shown to be part of an output circuit regulating rest:activity rhythms (Cavanaugh et al., 2014), and clocks in the DN1s are known to mediate other circadian behaviors, such as aspects of the male sex drive rhythm (Fujii and Amrein 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expressing CYCΔ in the DN1s did not alter sxe1 rhythms or expression levels in the fat body.
source: Since expressing CLKΔ in the DN1s was lethal, we expressed dominant negative CYCLE, CYCΔ, in the DN1s and found the manipulation did not alter sxe1 rhythms or expression levels in the fat body (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The six LNds express NPF (neuropeptide F), sNPF (short neuropeptide F), and ITP (ion transport peptide) in different cells, with some overlap.
source: The six LNds express NPF (neuropeptide F), sNPF (short neuropeptide F), and ITP (ion transport peptide) in different cells, with some overlap (Muraro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In adult males, NPF is expressed in 3 out of 6 LNds, as well as a subset of the LNvs and some non-clock neurons in the brain.
source: In adult males, NPF is expressed in 3 out of 6 LNds, as well as a subset of the LNvs and some non-clock neurons in the brain (Lee et al., 2006; Hermann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPF is expressed in endocrine cells in the midgut.
source: NPF is also expressed in endocrine cells in the midgut, although the role of NPF in these cells is not known (Brown et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 severely disrupted expression of sxe1.
source: Interestingly, we found that expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 severely disrupted expression of sxe1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: sxe1 expression was abolished using CYCΔ to disrupt clocks in NPF cells.
source: This effect was not specific to the CLKΔ transgene, because sxe1 expression was also abolished using CYCΔ to disrupt clocks in NPF cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A subset of the LNd cluster can be targeted with the Dvpdf-GAL4 driver in combination with pdf-GAL80.
source: A subset of the LNd cluster can also be targeted with the Dvpdf-GAL4 driver in combination with pdf-GAL80 (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expressing CLKΔ under Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 reduced sxe1 levels throughout most of the day, particularly at ZT16, the time of peak sxe1 expression.
source: Expressing CLKΔ under Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 reduced sxe1 levels throughout most of the day, particularly at ZT16, the time of peak sxe1 expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Dvpdf-GAL4 driver does not target all the NPF clock neurons.
source: The manipulation did not completely abolish rhythmic expression of sxe1, presumably because the Dvpdf-GAL4 driver does not target all the NPF clock neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete effect of Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 on sxe1 expression.

claim: Fat body expression of Cyp6a21 robustly cycles in wild type flies.
source: Fat body expression of Cyp6a21 robustly cycles in wild type flies but rhythmic expression was dampened in Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies, with a relatively small reduction in its overall expression level (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 was dampened in Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies, with a relatively small reduction in its overall expression level.
source: Fat body expression of Cyp6a21 robustly cycles in wild type flies but rhythmic expression was dampened in Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies, with a relatively small reduction in its overall expression level (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Clocks in NPF-positive neurons have a broader role in regulating the expression of cytochrome P450 genes in the fat body.
source: This suggests that clocks in NPF-positive neurons have a broader role in regulating the expression of cytochrome P450 genes in the fat body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both sxe1 and Cyp6a21 are affected by disrupting clocks in NPF neurons.

claim: Ablating clocks in NPF-positive cells did not alter rhythmic expression of per in the fat body.
source: Furthermore, ablating clocks in NPF-positive cells did not alter rhythmic expression of per, indicating that while rhythmic transcriptional output was impaired, the fat body clock remained intact (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: While rhythmic transcriptional output was impaired in Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies, the fat body clock remained intact.
source: Furthermore, ablating clocks in NPF-positive cells did not alter rhythmic expression of per, indicating that while rhythmic transcriptional output was impaired, the fat body clock remained intact (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that per rhythms persist in the fat body when NPF clocks are disrupted.

claim: A subset of LNds expressing NPF drive rhythmic expression of specific fat body genes.
source: Together, these data suggest that a subset of LNds expressing NPF drive rhythmic expression of specific fat body genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that disrupting clocks in NPF neurons affects specific fat body genes.

claim: After shifting flies to 30°C, expression of sxe1 remained rhythmic and similar to 18°C controls.
source: We found that after shifting flies to 30°C, expression of sxe1 remained rhythmic and similar to 18°C controls, suggesting adult-specific clock ablation in NPF-positive neurons is either incomplete or insufficient to affect sxe1 rhythms (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Adult-specific clock ablation in NPF-positive neurons is either incomplete or insufficient to affect sxe1 rhythms.
source: We found that after shifting flies to 30°C, expression of sxe1 remained rhythmic and similar to 18°C controls, suggesting adult-specific clock ablation in NPF-positive neurons is either incomplete or insufficient to affect sxe1 rhythms (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that adult-specific clock ablation does not affect sxe1 rhythms.

claim: Rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 was dampened by adult-specific clock ablation in LNd neurons.
source: However, this manipulation had a different effect on cyclic expression of Cyp6a21. Robust cycling of Cyp6a21 cycling was maintained in control flies kept at the permissive temperature, although the phase was shifted, perhaps due to the different temperature (18°C) required for this assay. Importantly though, rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 was dampened by adult-specific clock ablation in LNd neurons (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Clocks in NPF-expressing neurons have differential effects on the expression of cycling fat body genes.
source: Together these data indicate that clocks in NPF-expressing neurons have differential effects on the expression of cycling fat body genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of adult-specific clock ablation on sxe1 versus Cyp6a21.

claim: NPF was reported to cycle in a subset of NPF-positive neurons, including LNds and LNvs.
source: Indeed, NPF was reported to cycle in a subset of NPF-positive neurons, including LNds and LNvs (He et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF regulates feeding in Drosophila.
source: NPF regulates a variety of behavioral processes in Drosophila including feeding (Wu et al., 2003; 2005; Lingo et al., 2007; Itskov and Ribeiro, 2013), courtship (Kim et al., 2013), aggression (Dierick and Greenspan, 2007), and sleep (He et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPF regulates courtship in Drosophila.
source: NPF regulates a variety of behavioral processes in Drosophila including feeding (Wu et al., 2003; 2005; Lingo et al., 2007; Itskov and Ribeiro, 2013), courtship (Kim et al., 2013), aggression (Dierick and Greenspan, 2007), and sleep (He et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF regulates aggression in Drosophila.
source: NPF regulates a variety of behavioral processes in Drosophila including feeding (Wu et al., 2003; 2005; Lingo et al., 2007; Itskov and Ribeiro, 2013), courtship (Kim et al., 2013), aggression (Dierick and Greenspan, 2007), and sleep (He et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF regulates sleep in Drosophila.
source: NPF regulates a variety of behavioral processes in Drosophila including feeding (Wu et al., 2003; 2005; Lingo et al., 2007; Itskov and Ribeiro, 2013), courtship (Kim et al., 2013), aggression (Dierick and Greenspan, 2007), and sleep (He et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Flies expressing CLKΔ with Npf-GAL4 display normal rhythms of rest:activity.
source: We found that flies expressing CLKΔ with Npf-GAL4 as well as flies carrying a null mutation in nfpr, the gene encoding the receptor for NPF, display normal rhythms of rest:activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Flies carrying a null mutation in npfr display normal rhythms of rest:activity.
source: We found that flies expressing CLKΔ with Npf-GAL4 as well as flies carrying a null mutation in nfpr, the gene encoding the receptor for NPF, display normal rhythms of rest:activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 driving UAS-CLKΔ increased the number of arrhythmic flies and slightly lengthened the period of rhythmic flies.
source: In contrast, Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 driving UAS-CLKΔ increased the number of arrhythmic flies and slightly lengthened the period of rhythmic flies, further indicating that Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 and Npf-GAL4 do not represent the exact same population of LNds (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 and Npf-GAL4 do not represent the exact same population of LNds.
source: In contrast, Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 driving UAS-CLKΔ increased the number of arrhythmic flies and slightly lengthened the period of rhythmic flies, further indicating that Dvpdf-GAL4;pdf-GAL80 and Npf-GAL4 do not represent the exact same population of LNds (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the different behavioral effects of disrupting clocks with these two drivers.

claim: NPF plays at best a minor role in regulating rhythmic locomotor behavior.
source: These data suggest that NPF plays at best a minor role in regulating rhythmic locomotor behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting NPF signaling does not affect rest:activity rhythms.

claim: Driving UAS-npf RNAi under Npf-GAL4 resulted in dampened but still rhythmic sxe1 expression.
source: Driving UAS-npf RNAi under Npf-GAL4 resulted in dampened but still rhythmic sxe1 expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Driving UAS-npf RNAi under Npf-GAL4 vastly reduced npf levels in fly heads.
source: Although this manipulation vastly reduced npf levels in fly heads (Figure 4B), it is possible that very small amounts of NPF can drive some level of cycling; alternatively, knockdown efficiency may have been limited in the NPF-positive clock cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: sxe1 levels do not cycle and are dramatically reduced in npfr mutants.
source: Our results show sxe1 levels do not cycle and are dramatically reduced in npfr mutants, which phenocopies the daily sxe1 expression profile of flies expressing either CLKΔ or CYCΔ under Npf-GAL4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 was lost in the fat body of npfr mutants.
source: Rhythmic expression of Cyp6a21 was also lost in the fat body of npfr mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 alters the circadian production or release of NPF.
source: We speculate that expressing CLKΔ under Npf-GAL4 alters the circadian production or release of NPF.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed effects of clock disruption in NPF neurons.

claim: mRNA analysis of Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ heads showed that npf levels were reduced compared to controls.
source: Indeed, mRNA analysis of Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ heads showed that npf levels were reduced compared to controls (Figure 4E) while cyclic per expression, which arises from clock function in many different cells, was unaffected (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cyclic per expression in heads was unaffected in Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ flies.
source: Indeed, mRNA analysis of Npf-GAL4/UAS-CLKΔ heads showed that npf levels were reduced compared to controls (Figure 4E) while cyclic per expression, which arises from clock function in many different cells, was unaffected (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Loss of NPF expression occurs in LNds of Clkjrk brains.
source: This result is consistent with reports of loss of NPF expression in LNds of Clkjrk brains (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Circadian clocks in NPF-positive cells regulate NPF expression to subsequently drive sxe1 and Cyp6a21 rhythms in the fat body.
source: Taken together, these data suggest circadian clocks in NPF-positive cells regulate NPF expression to subsequently drive sxe1 and Cyp6a21 rhythms in the fat body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that both clock function in NPF neurons and NPF signaling are required for sxe1 and Cyp6a21 rhythms.

claim: Liver-specific circadian clocks play an important role in liver physiology via contributions to glucose homeostasis and xenobiotic clearance.
source: In mammals, liver-specific circadian clocks play an important role in liver physiology via contributions to glucose homeostasis and xenobiotic clearance (Gachon et al., 2006; Lamia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Liver clock ablation in mice resembles fat body clock ablation in flies.
source: Liver clock ablation in mice resembles fat body clock ablation in flies; in particular, ablating liver clocks eliminates rhythmic expression of most, but not all, circadian liver transcripts (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ablating liver clocks eliminates rhythmic expression of most, but not all, circadian liver transcripts.
source: Liver clock ablation in mice resembles fat body clock ablation in flies; in particular, ablating liver clocks eliminates rhythmic expression of most, but not all, circadian liver transcripts (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Rescuing clock function specifically in the brains of ClockΔ19 mutant mice restores rhythmic expression of roughly 40% of circadian liver transcripts.
source: Furthermore, rescuing clock function specifically in the brains of ClockΔ19 mutant mice restores rhythmic expression of roughly 40% of circadian liver transcripts (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Some circadian transcripts in the liver are driven by systemic signals, perhaps emanating from the master pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus.
source: These data suggest that some circadian transcripts in the liver are driven by systemic signals, perhaps emanating from the master pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus (Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that brain clocks can restore some liver rhythms, supported by citation.

claim: Cyp2b10 continues to cycle in animals lacking functional liver clocks.
source: Although there is no direct mammalian homologue of sxe1, we noticed that a similar P450 enzyme involved in xenobiotic detoxification, Cyp2b10, also continues to cycle in animals lacking functional liver clocks (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cyp2b10 transcript levels did not display a circadian rhythm in Npy KOs.
source: We measured Cyp2b10 levels in Npy KO and wild type mice and found that Cyp2b10 transcript levels did not display a circadian rhythm in Npy KOs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Circadian expression of Rev-erb alpha was unaffected in the livers of Npy KOs.
source: However, circadian expression of the core clock gene Rev-erb alpha was unaffected in the livers of Npy KOs confirming that the liver clock is still intact (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The liver clock is still intact in Npy KOs.
source: However, circadian expression of the core clock gene Rev-erb alpha was unaffected in the livers of Npy KOs confirming that the liver clock is still intact (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rev-erb alpha rhythms persist in Npy KOs.

claim: Alas1 is required for P450 synthesis.
source: Aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (Alas1), is required for P450 synthesis (Furuyama et al., 2007) and was also reported to cycle in the absence of the liver clock (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Alas1 was reported to cycle in the absence of the liver clock.
source: Aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (Alas1), is required for P450 synthesis (Furuyama et al., 2007) and was also reported to cycle in the absence of the liver clock (Kornmann et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Circadian expression of Alas1 was unaffected in Npy KOs.
source: Unlike Cyp2b10, circadian expression of Alas1 was unaffected in Npy KOs, suggesting that NPY does not regulate global rhythmic detoxification in the liver (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: NPY does not regulate global rhythmic detoxification in the liver.
source: Unlike Cyp2b10, circadian expression of Alas1 was unaffected in Npy KOs, suggesting that NPY does not regulate global rhythmic detoxification in the liver (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Alas1 rhythms persist in Npy KOs while Cyp2b10 rhythms do not.

claim: 289 transcripts were cyclic in controls but not in Npy KO.
source: Using the newly developed MetaCycle package (see Materials and methods) and a stringent P-value cutoff of p<0.01 to detect cyclic transcripts, we found that 289 transcripts were cyclic in controls but not in Npy KO, indicating that the oscillation of these transcripts is under the regulation of Npy signaling (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The oscillation of 289 transcripts is under the regulation of Npy signaling.
source: Using the newly developed MetaCycle package (see Materials and methods) and a stringent P-value cutoff of p<0.01 to detect cyclic transcripts, we found that 289 transcripts were cyclic in controls but not in Npy KO, indicating that the oscillation of these transcripts is under the regulation of Npy signaling (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these transcripts cycle in wild type but not in Npy KO.

claim: The loss of transcript cycling was generally not accompanied by differences in expression levels in Npy KO.
source: Furthermore, the loss of transcript cycling was generally not accompanied by differences in expression levels; in other words, the median transcript abundance in wild type animals correlated with that in Npy KO (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cyp2r1, Cyp17a1, and Cyp2c70 transcripts cycle in wild type but not in Npy KO liver.
source: Notably, the microarray data confirmed our qPCR data for Cyp2b10 and indicated that Cyp2r1, Cyp17a1, and Cyp2c70 transcripts also cycle in wild type but not in Npy KO liver.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cyp3a13 and Cyp7a1 transcripts cycle robustly in both wild type and Npy KO genotypes.
source: In contrast, Cyp3a13 and Cyp7a1 transcripts cycle robustly in both genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Nine liver clock-independent transcripts require Npy for robust rhythmic expression: Rbl2, Ddx46, Cirbp, Sqle, Ldb1, Actg1, Hmgcs1, Heca, and Ctgf.
source: Among that set, we discovered nine additional liver clock-independent transcripts—Rbl2, Ddx46, Cirbp, Sqle, Ldb1, Actg1, Hmgcs1, Heca, and Ctgf—that require Npy for robust rhythmic expression (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Only a subset of liver-clock independent transcripts requires Npy for oscillations.
source: As only a subset of liver-clock independent transcripts requires Npy for oscillations, other mechanisms likely contribute to rhythmic expression of these genes (further discussed below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that not all liver clock-independent genes require Npy.

claim: The overall phases and amplitudes of expression for cycling transcripts in Npy KO slightly differed from those in wild type.
source: Although many genes, including clock genes, continued to cycle in Npy knockout livers, the overall phases and amplitudes of expression for cycling transcripts in Npy KO slightly differed from those in wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diverse liver circadian transcripts, including cytochrome P450 genes, are influenced by Npy signaling.
source: Overall we found that diverse liver circadian transcripts, including cytochrome P450 genes, are influenced by Npy signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microarray data showing multiple genes affected by Npy.

claim: This report is the first to describe a role for Npy in the circadian regulation of peripheral gene expression in mammals.
source: This report is the first to describe a role for Npy in the circadian regulation of peripheral gene expression in mammals.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in this study.

claim: Clocks in PDF-positive neurons influence cycling of the per clock gene in the Drosophila fat body in the absence of external cues.
source: We find that clocks in PDF-positive neurons influence cycling of the per clock gene in the Drosophila fat body in the absence of external cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Clocks in Drosophila NPF-positive neurons drive daily expression of sxe1 and Cyp6a21, fat body genes not controlled by the fat body clock.
source: We show that clocks in Drosophila NPF-positive neurons drive daily expression of sxe1 and Cyp6a21, fat body genes not controlled by the fat body clock.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Mammalian Npy drives rhythmic expression of specific liver transcripts.
source: Likewise, mammalian Npy drives rhythmic expression of specific liver transcripts, indicating a conserved role of NPF/Npy in the control of peripheral circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: NPF/Npy has a conserved role in the control of peripheral circadian rhythms.
source: Likewise, mammalian Npy drives rhythmic expression of specific liver transcripts, indicating a conserved role of NPF/Npy in the control of peripheral circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the parallel findings in flies and mice.

claim: It was proposed that clocks in the brain and fat body interact.
source: Prior to this report, it was proposed that clocks in the brain and fat body interact, but the extent of the interaction and the mechanisms driving it were not identified (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In light:dark cycles, the central clock is not required for cycling of the fat body clock.
source: Our data suggest that in light:dark cycles, the central clock is not required for cycling of the fat body clock, although we cannot exclude an effect on the phase of cycling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing per rhythms persist in LD when PDF neurons lack functional clocks.

claim: In constant conditions, the clock in PDF cells influences the fat body clock.
source: However, in constant conditions, the clock in PDF cells influences the fat body clock, as it does the prothoracic gland clock.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of per rhythms in DD when PDF neurons lack functional clocks.

claim: The fat body clock modulates behavioral rhythms, specifically the phase of feeding rhythms.
source: Unlike other peripheral clocks, the fat body clock modulates behavioral rhythms, specifically the phase of feeding rhythms, in addition to its own physiology (Xu et al., 2008; 2011; Seay and Thummel, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Synchrony between clocks in the brain and fat body is likely essential for metabolic homeostasis.
source: Thus, synchrony between clocks in the brain and fat body is likely essential for metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that brain and fat body clocks interact and both affect metabolism.

claim: Tissue-specific gene expression patterns are thought to be generated primarily by local clocks.
source: Tissue-specific gene expression patterns are thought to be generated primarily by local clocks; however, few studies have comprehensively evaluated rhythmic expression driven by local clocks versus external factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Disrupting clocks in NPF-positive cells abolished rhythmic expression of two cytochrome P450 genes, sxe1 and Cyp6a21.
source: Here we report that at least some of the other 40% of circadian fat body genes are regulated by clocks located in other tissues. We found that disrupting clocks in NPF-positive cells abolished rhythmic expression of two cytochrome P450 genes, sxe1 and Cyp6a21.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: It is unlikely the LNvs regulate sxe1 rhythms, because disrupting clocks in PDF-positive LNvs does not abolish sxe1 oscillations.
source: In addition, even though NPF expression has been reported in both the LNds and LNvs (Hermann et al., 2012), it is unlikely the LNvs regulate sxe1 rhythms, because disrupting clocks in PDF-positive LNvs does not abolish sxe1 oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that disrupting PDF neurons does not abolish sxe1 rhythms.

claim: LNds can be synchronized by inputs from LNvs.
source: LNds can be synchronized by inputs from LNvs (Guo et al., 2014), but cell-autonomous entrainment mechanisms in the LNds may limit the influence of LNvs in light:dark cycles, which may explain why ablating clocks in LNvs has a small effect on sxe1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cell-autonomous entrainment mechanisms in the LNds may limit the influence of LNvs in light:dark cycles.
source: LNds can be synchronized by inputs from LNvs (Guo et al., 2014), but cell-autonomous entrainment mechanisms in the LNds may limit the influence of LNvs in light:dark cycles, which may explain why ablating clocks in LNvs has a small effect on sxe1 expression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The clocks in LNds are required for cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 expression in the fat body.
source: Thus, we suggest that the clocks in LNds are required for cycling of sxe1 and Cyp6a21 expression in the fat body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that disrupting clocks in LNds affects these genes.

claim: NPF neuropeptide reportedly modulates rest:activity rhythms in Drosophila.
source: NPF neuropeptide reportedly modulates rest:activity rhythms in Drosophila (Hermann et al., 2012; He et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flies lacking functional clocks in NPF cells display significantly reduced npf levels.
source: Consistent with the assertion that NPF is the relevant output for fat body rhythms from NPF-positive cells, we also found that flies lacking functional clocks in these cells display significantly reduced npf levels (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E (note: text says 4D but refers to npf levels which is shown in 4E).

claim: npf mRNA is absent in the LNds of adult male Clkjrk mutant brains.
source: Interestingly, Lee et al. previously showed that npf mRNA is absent in the LNds of adult male Clkjrk mutant brains (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF is regulated by the circadian clock in LNds, and its release from these neurons is necessary for mRNA rhythms of specific fat body genes.
source: This further supports our hypothesis that NPF is regulated by the circadian clock in LNds, and its release from these neurons is necessary for mRNA rhythms of specific fat body genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: The effect of NPF on the fat body is likely not direct.
source: However, the effect of NPF on the fat body is likely not direct.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about NPF signaling in Drosophila.

claim: Some insect species release NPF into the hemolymph to reach other tissues, but this does not appear to be the case in Drosophila.
source: Some insect species release NPF into the hemolymph to reach other tissues, but this does not appear to be the case in Drosophila (Nässel and Wegener, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF-positive clock neurons drive rhythmic gene expression in the fat body, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the pathway(s) that convey circadian information from the brain to peripheral tissues.
source: Our discovery that NPF-positive clock neurons drive rhythmic gene expression in the fat body provides a unique opportunity to investigate the pathway(s) that convey circadian information from the brain to peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Npy is not required for free-running rest:activity rhythms in mice.
source: Npy is not required for free-running rest:activity rhythms in mice, but it promotes phase shifts in these rhythms in response to non-photic stimuli (Yannielli and Harrington, 2004; Maywood et al., 2002; Besing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Npy promotes phase shifts in rest:activity rhythms in response to non-photic stimuli in mice.
source: Npy is not required for free-running rest:activity rhythms in mice, but it promotes phase shifts in these rhythms in response to non-photic stimuli (Yannielli and Harrington, 2004; Maywood et al., 2002; Besing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Behavioral effects of Npy are likely mediated by its brain expression.
source: Behavioral effects of Npy are likely mediated by its brain expression, but as Npy is also expressed in the periphery, it is possible that a peripheral source contributes to cycling in the liver.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on knowledge about Npy expression.

claim: Npy has a profound effect on circadian gene expression in the liver.
source: Regardless, it is clear that Npy has a profound effect on circadian gene expression in the liver.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the microarray data.

claim: NPF promotes feeding in Drosophila larvae.
source: Since NPF promotes feeding in Drosophila larvae (Wu et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2005; Lingo et al., 2007) and Npy does so in mice, it is possible NPF/Npy drive cycling in the fat body/liver through the regulation of feeding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Npy promotes feeding in mice.
source: Since NPF promotes feeding in Drosophila larvae (Wu et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2005; Lingo et al., 2007) and Npy does so in mice, it is possible NPF/Npy drive cycling in the fat body/liver through the regulation of feeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Npy function.

claim: Feeding is known to be a potent stimulus for metabolic clocks.
source: Feeding is known to be a potent stimulus for metabolic clocks, with circadian gene expression in peripheral tissues driven by restricted feeding cycles in both flies and mammals (Xu et al., 2011; Gill et al., 2015; Vollmers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Under conditions of ad lib food, feeding rhythms in flies are of low amplitude and likely insufficient to drive robust cycling.
source: However, under conditions of ad lib food, feeding rhythms in flies are of low amplitude and likely insufficient to drive robust cycling.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about feeding rhythms in flies.

claim: Cyclic expression of Cyp6a21 can be driven by a restricted feeding paradigm.
source: Consistent with this, while cyclic expression of Cyp6a21 can be driven by a restricted feeding paradigm, as can the clock in the fat body, cycling is more robust when this paradigm is conducted in wild type versus clockless animals (Xu et al., 2011), indicating that its regulation is not through feeding alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Regulation of Cyp6a21 is not through feeding alone.
source: Consistent with this, while cyclic expression of Cyp6a21 can be driven by a restricted feeding paradigm, as can the clock in the fat body, cycling is more robust when this paradigm is conducted in wild type versus clockless animals (Xu et al., 2011), indicating that its regulation is not through feeding alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Cyp6a21 cycling is more robust in wild type than clockless animals under restricted feeding.

claim: Time restricted feeding experiments of mice do not support the idea that restricted feeding drives cycling of Cyp2b10 in clockless mice.
source: Finally, time restricted feeding experiments of mice do not support the idea that restricted feeding drives cycling of Cyp2b10 in clockless mice, even though it is sufficient to maintain rhythms of many other liver genes (Vollmers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: These genes (sxe1, Cyp6a21, Cyp2b10) are unique in their dependence on Npy.
source: Thus, while feeding cannot be discounted as an important factor, which may contribute to the cycling of the genes reported here, these genes are unique in their dependence on Npy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing specific dependence on NPF/Npy.

claim: Several fly genes, for example sxe2 and CG17562, continue to oscillate when CLKΔ is expressed under Npf-GAL4.
source: Similarly, several fly genes, for example sxe2 and CG17562, continue to oscillate when CLKΔ is expressed under Npf-GAL4 (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished experimental data.

claim: There are additional mechanisms regulating circadian rhythms in the fat body/liver beyond NPF/Npy.
source: These results suggest there are additional mechanisms regulating circadian rhythms in the fat body/liver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that not all clock-independent genes require NPF/Npy.

claim: Different mechanisms may regulate distinct phases of circadian gene expression.
source: Why would more than one mechanism exist to couple rhythmic gene expression in a specific peripheral tissue to other clocks? One possibility is that different mechanisms regulate distinct phases of circadian gene expression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible explanations for multiple mechanisms.

claim: Different mechanisms may couple gene expression to different cell populations, processes, or behaviors.
source: Alternatively, different mechanisms may couple gene expression to different cell populations, processes, or behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible explanations for multiple mechanisms.

claim: Cytochrome P450 genes, such as Cyp6a21, sxe1 and Cyp2b10, are associated with detoxification.
source: Cytochrome P450 genes, such as Cyp6a21, sxe1 and Cyp2b10, are associated with detoxification (King-Jones et al., 2006; Fujii et al., 2008), which is likely rhythmic, although not yet reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Detoxification is likely rhythmic.
source: Cytochrome P450 genes, such as Cyp6a21, sxe1 and Cyp2b10, are associated with detoxification (King-Jones et al., 2006; Fujii et al., 2008), which is likely rhythmic, although not yet reported.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the rhythmic expression of detoxification genes.

claim: Overexpression of NPFR in larvae increases foraging behavior as well as consumption of noxious or bitter compounds.
source: Overexpression of NPFR in larvae increases foraging behavior as well as consumption of noxious or bitter compounds (Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: NPF/Npy signaling is generally associated with an increase in feeding.
source: Indeed, NPF/Npy signaling is generally associated with an increase in feeding (Wu et al., 2003; 2005; Lingo et al., 2007; Beck, 2006), which can lead to ingestion of toxic substances.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Coordination of feeding with expression of detoxification enzymes through NPF/Npy may have evolved to promote survival.
source: Thus, coordination of feeding with expression of detoxification enzymes, such as sxe1, Cyp6a21 and Cyp2b10, through NPF/Npy may have evolved to promote survival.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: Large delays between consumption of noxious substances and their removal could affect an animal's health.
source: Large delays between consumption of noxious substances and their removal could affect an animal's health; thus, the need for coordination between clocks in processing such substances.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of coordination.

claim: Conservation of cytochrome P450 regulation from flies to mammals supports the idea that neural control of detoxification in the periphery promotes organismal fitness.
source: Conservation of cytochrome P450 regulation from flies to mammals supports the idea that neural control of detoxification in the periphery promotes organismal fitness (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the mechanism across species.

claim: NPF/Npy and sxe1/Cyp2b10 expression is sexually dimorphic in Drosophila and mammals.
source: Interestingly, NPF/Npy and sxe1/Cyp2b10 expression is sexually dimorphic in Drosophila (Lee et al., 2006; Fujii et al., 2008) and mammals (Lu et al., 2013; Karl et al., 2008; Urban et al., 1993), suggesting there may be some gender specificity to this entire pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There may be some gender specificity to the NPF/Npy pathway regulating cytochrome P450 genes.
source: Interestingly, NPF/Npy and sxe1/Cyp2b10 expression is sexually dimorphic in Drosophila (Lee et al., 2006; Fujii et al., 2008) and mammals (Lu et al., 2013; Karl et al., 2008; Urban et al., 1993), suggesting there may be some gender specificity to this entire pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sexual dimorphism of the genes involved.

claim: Rhythmic expression of genes involved in drug breakdown and absorption in the liver influences drug efficacy and toxicity.
